title: Testing Basics
summary: Write code that checks your code: arrange, act, assert, edge cases, exceptions and fakes.

steps.title: A test is just code
body: A **test** is a small method that calls your code and complains if the result is wrong. Run all the tests after every change and you know at once whether you broke something.
Nearly every test has the same three parts:
// Act: do the one thing being tested
Real projects use a framework such as xUnit to find and run tests. Frameworks are NuGet packages, so this lesson uses a tiny stand-in with the same feel. It is available in every code step here:
Assert.Equal(expected, actual);          // fails unless the two are equal
Assert.True(condition);                  // fails unless the condition is true
Assert.Throws<TException>(() => ...);    // fails unless the code throws that exception
*Fails* means *throws an exception*. A test passes when it runs to the end without throwing.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a test in arrange, act, assert order.
steps.explain: Set up the object, call the method under test once, then compare what came back with what you expected.

steps.prompt: In the test above, which line is the **Act** step?
steps.explain: The test is about `Total`. Creating the cart and adding an item only prepare for that call, and the assert checks its result.

steps.title: Your first test
prompt: A shop charges **4.99** for shipping, but orders of **50 or more** ship free.
Write the test `static void TestShippingCost(Func<decimal, decimal> shippingCost)`. The parameter is the function under test: `shippingCost(orderTotal)` returns the shipping cost.
Your test must:
- pass when it is given a correct implementation
- fail (an `Assert` throws) when it is given a broken one
The grader will run your test against one correct implementation and two broken ones: one that never charges, and one that always charges.
template: Dojo.Check("Your test passes for the correct ShippingCost", __good == null, "It failed with: " + __good);
Dojo.Check("Your test fails for a version that never charges", __Run(total => 0m) != null, "Assert the cost of a small order.");
Dojo.Check("Your test fails for a version that always charges", __Run(total => 4.99m) != null, "Assert the cost of a large order.");
class AssertFailedException : Exception { public AssertFailedException(string message) : base(message) { } }
public static void Equal<T>(T expected, T actual)
if (!condition) throw new AssertFailedException("Expected the condition to be true");
public static void Throws<TException>(Action action) where TException : Exception
catch (Exception e) { throw new AssertFailedException($"Expected {typeof(TException).Name} but got {e.GetType().Name}"); }
throw new AssertFailedException($"Expected {typeof(TException).Name} but nothing was thrown");
hints: One assert is not enough: a function that always returns the same number would satisfy it.
Check a small order and a large one. Remember the `m` suffix for decimals.

steps.title: Edge cases and exceptions
body: Bugs rarely live in the middle of the range. They live at the **edges**:
- the exact boundary (is an order of exactly 50 free?)
- the largest value allowed, and one past it
A classic bug is writing `>` where `>=` was meant. Only a test *at* the boundary can see it.
Throwing is behaviour too, so test it. `Assert.Throws` runs a lambda and fails unless it throws the exception you named:
For each rule in the specification, ask: *what is the nearest input that should behave differently?* Test both sides.

steps.prompt: `Withdraw(balance, amount)` returns the new balance. It throws when `amount` is zero or negative, and when `amount` is more than `balance`. What kind of test case is each call?
steps.explain: The interesting tests sit right next to each rule: exactly the balance works, one cent more throws; one cent works, zero throws.

steps.prompt: A test runner is only a `try`/`catch` around each test. What does this program print?
steps.explain: The second test fails its assertion. The third never reaches the assertion: `int.Parse("x")` throws, and any unexpected exception also counts as a failed test.

steps.title: Hunt the bugs
prompt: `withdraw(balance, amount)` should follow these rules:
- `amount` zero or negative: throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`
- `amount` greater than `balance`: throws `InvalidOperationException`
- otherwise: returns `balance - amount`. Taking out the whole balance is allowed.
Write `static void TestWithdraw(Func<decimal, decimal, decimal> withdraw)`.
The grader runs it against a correct implementation and **four** subtly broken ones. Your test must pass for the correct one and fail for each broken one. Think about the edges.
starter: static void TestWithdraw(Func<decimal, decimal, decimal> withdraw)
// TODO: this one typical case is not enough. Add the edges.
solution: static void TestWithdraw(Func<decimal, decimal, decimal> withdraw)
template: if (amount > balance) throw new InvalidOperationException("Insufficient funds");
Dojo.Check("Your test passes for the correct Withdraw", __good == null, "It failed with: " + __good);
Dojo.Check("Your test catches a version that lets you overdraw", __Run((balance, amount) =>
}) != null, "Assert that taking out more than the balance throws InvalidOperationException.");
Dojo.Check("Your test catches a version that refuses to empty the account", __Run((balance, amount) =>
if (amount >= balance) throw new InvalidOperationException("Insufficient funds");
}) != null, "Withdraw exactly the balance and assert that the result is 0.");
Dojo.Check("Your test catches a version that accepts a negative amount", __Run((balance, amount) =>
if (amount > balance) throw new InvalidOperationException("Insufficient funds");
}) != null, "Assert that a negative amount throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.");
Dojo.Check("Your test catches a version that accepts an amount of zero", __Run((balance, amount) =>
if (amount > balance) throw new InvalidOperationException("Insufficient funds");
}) != null, "Assert that an amount of exactly 0 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.");
class AssertFailedException : Exception { public AssertFailedException(string message) : base(message) { } }
public static void Equal<T>(T expected, T actual)
if (!condition) throw new AssertFailedException("Expected the condition to be true");
public static void Throws<TException>(Action action) where TException : Exception
catch (Exception e) { throw new AssertFailedException($"Expected {typeof(TException).Name} but got {e.GetType().Name}"); }
throw new AssertFailedException($"Expected {typeof(TException).Name} but nothing was thrown");
hints: There are two rules that throw, and each has a boundary. That suggests at least four more asserts.
Exactly the balance must work: `Assert.Equal(0m, withdraw(100m, 100m));`. One cent more must throw.
`Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => withdraw(100m, 0m));` and the same again for `-5m`. Zero and negative are different bugs.

steps.title: What makes code testable
body: A test can only control what goes **in through the front door**: constructor arguments and method parameters. Code is hard to test when it reaches out for things on its own:
int days = (DateTime.Today - due).Days;     // a hidden input
This gives a different answer every day, so no fixed assert can be right for long. The clock, random numbers, files, the network and the database are all hidden inputs like this.
The cure is the one from the last lesson: put the hidden input behind an interface and pass it in.
static decimal LateFee(IClock clock, DateTime due)

A test passes a **fake** clock stuck on a date it chose. Fakes make tests fast and repeatable. Keep a few tests that use the **real** dependency as well, because a fake only proves your code works with what you *believe* the real thing does.

steps.prompt: Each line on the left makes code hard to test. Match it to the fake a test would pass in instead.
pairs: a clock that always returns the same moment
a number source that returns a fixed sequence
an in-memory dictionary of file names to text
a client that returns canned JSON without a network

steps.title: Due soon, with its own tests
prompt: **Sidekick piece: due soon, tested.** `sk` warns "2 tasks are due within 2 days", and `sk selftest` runs the tests you write here. Your `TaskItem` and `Sk.Today(TimeProvider)` (from Dates and time) are given.
Write three things:
1. `class FixedClock : TimeProvider`: a constructor `FixedClock(DateTimeOffset now)`, `GetUtcNow()` returns `now`, and `LocalTimeZone` is `TimeZoneInfo.Utc` (so "today" never depends on the machine).

2. `static bool IsDueSoon(TaskItem task, TimeProvider clock, int withinDays)`: false for a finished task or one with no `Due`; otherwise true when the due date is at most `withinDays` days after `Sk.Today(clock)` (overdue counts as soon).

3. `static List<string> DueSoonChecks()`: **your own tests**. Use a `FixedClock` and at least six checks (due today, at the limit, one past it, overdue, no due date, finished). Return the names of the checks that fail, so an empty list means all pass. A local helper keeps it short:
```csharp
var failures = new List<string>();
void Check(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failures.Add(name); }
Write the two methods first and `FixedClock` at the bottom.
starter: static bool IsDueSoon(TaskItem task, TimeProvider clock, int withinDays)
void Check(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failures.Add(name); }
// a FixedClock, then six or more checks
solution: static bool IsDueSoon(TaskItem task, TimeProvider clock, int withinDays)
if (task.Done || task.Due is not DateOnly due) return false;
void Check(string name, bool ok) { if (!ok) failures.Add(name); }
var clock = new FixedClock(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 25, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
TaskItem DueIn(int days) => new TaskItem(1, "Ship it") { Due = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25).AddDays(days) };
Check("due today is soon", IsDueSoon(DueIn(0), clock, 2));
Check("due in 2 days is soon", IsDueSoon(DueIn(2), clock, 2));
Check("due in 3 days is not soon", !IsDueSoon(DueIn(3), clock, 2));
Check("no due date is never soon", !IsDueSoon(new TaskItem(2, "Someday"), clock, 2));
Check("a finished task is not soon", !IsDueSoon(finished, clock, 2));
template: Dojo.Eq("FixedClock gives back the time it was made with", dojoNow, dojoClock.GetUtcNow());
Dojo.Eq("Sk.Today on your FixedClock is that day", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25), Sk.Today(dojoClock));
TaskItem DojoDue(int days) => new TaskItem(5, "Report") { Due = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25).AddDays(days) };
Dojo.Check("due today is soon", IsDueSoon(DojoDue(0), dojoClock, 2), "expected true");
Dojo.Check("due in 2 days is soon (within 2)", IsDueSoon(DojoDue(2), dojoClock, 2), "expected true");
Dojo.Check("due in 3 days is not soon (within 2)", !IsDueSoon(DojoDue(3), dojoClock, 2), "expected false");
Dojo.Check("due in 3 days is soon within 5", IsDueSoon(DojoDue(3), dojoClock, 5), "expected true");
Dojo.Check("4 days overdue counts as soon", IsDueSoon(DojoDue(-4), dojoClock, 2), "expected true");
Dojo.Check("no due date is never soon", !IsDueSoon(new TaskItem(6, "Someday"), dojoClock, 2), "expected false");
Dojo.Check("a finished task is never soon", !IsDueSoon(dojoDone, dojoClock, 2), "expected false");
Dojo.Eq("your DueSoonChecks all pass against your IsDueSoon", new List<string>(), DueSoonChecks());
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");

require.message: DueSoonChecks makes at least six checks
IsDueSoon asks Sk.Today for the date

hints: `FixedClock`: store `now` in a field; `public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => now;` and `public override TimeZoneInfo LocalTimeZone => TimeZoneInfo.Utc;`.
`IsDueSoon`: `if (task.Done || task.Due is not DateOnly due) return false;` then compare `due.DayNumber - Sk.Today(clock).DayNumber` with `withinDays`.
In `DueSoonChecks`, a helper `TaskItem DueIn(int days) => new TaskItem(1, "Ship it") { Due = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25).AddDays(days) };` makes each check one line.
steps.explain: Your tests never touch the real clock, so they pass on any day of the year. That is exactly why `sk` takes a `TimeProvider` instead of calling `DateTime.Now`: the real program passes `TimeProvider.System`, tests pass a `FixedClock`.
